The room smelled of old paper and turpentine, a dry, scholarly dust that seemed to have settled not in years but in centuries. He was bent over a great, scarred table under the single searching eye of a brass lamp, his spectacles perched so far down his nose they seemed in imminent danger of becoming a permanent fixture of his chin. He did not look up when I entered, but a hand, thin and stained with ink, waved me towards a chair that groaned in protest as I took it.

‘I was just remembering,’ he said, his voice a dry rustle like old parchment, and he straightened his back with a wince that was almost a theatrical performance. ‘I was remembering the day I finished this particular chart. Not a copy, you understand, but the original survey. All mine.’ He gestured with a fine-nibbed pen, a delicate instrument that seemed an extension of his own spidery fingers, towards the vast sheet of vellum pinned to the great table that consumed the centre of the room. It was a coastline, drawn with an artist’s love and a madman’s precision; every cove, every treacherous shoal, every faint suggestion of a river’s mouth was rendered in a detail that was at once beautiful and terrifying. ‘I had been in that filth for three years. I had buried two good men; I had bartered my soul for a cup of clean water more times than I could count; my own face in a piece of polished tin was a stranger to me. And then, back in a civilized room, with my data, my numbers…I put the last line on it. The last little symbol for a mangrove swamp.’

He took off his spectacles and began to polish them with a furious, concentrated energy, his eyes, suddenly naked and vulnerable, fixed on some point in the shadowed corner of the room. ‘When I saw it complete, the whole impossible coast held there, captured in my own ink…a feeling came over me. A power. It was as if I had not merely mapped the land, but created it. In the words of the navigator’ (he pronounced it “nafigador”)-- “‘Agora eu o seguro, o mundo inteiro em meu projeto, e chamo-o de certa forma meu.’” He spoke the last words in a whisper, a conspirator’s confession, and his gaze slid from the shadows to meet mine. ‘Yes, my friend. I had tamed a piece of the world that had very nearly killed me; I had a name for myself; I had the respect of men who mattered; I had a wife’ (he said “wiv”) ‘who waited, a house on a clean street--and this, this monster, this beautiful liar of a map, was mine too!’ He paused, his thumb tracing a phantom coastline on the arm of his chair. ‘“Husband, captain, father,” he said, his voice dropping low, his eyes on the invisible line he drew--“poof!” A little puff of air, and the gesture was done. He sighed and leaned back, the chair creaking a mournful complaint. The silence in the room was so profound I could hear the faint hiss of the lamp’s wick.

‘The work,’ he began again, his tone regaining its usual wry placidity as he gestured to my own dishevelled appearance, ‘does not seem to have gone well. You have the look of a man who has brought back bad news.’

‘To be perfectly honest, Alistair,’ I said, the words costing me a greater effort than I had anticipated, ‘I came here to report on a failed survey.’

‘Reefs where there should have been none?’ he asked, a flicker of professional interest in his eyes.

‘Something less tangible,’ I answered, feeling my confidence crumble into a fine, bitter dust. ‘A man!’

‘Ach so!’ he breathed, and the scholar’s curiosity in his face softened into a weary sort of compassion. He looked at me for a long moment, his head tilted. ‘Well--I am one of those too.’

There was in his manner a kind of profound, gentle gravity that invited the most painful truths; he made of his quiet study a confessional, and if one hesitated at the door, it was only out of a sudden, sharp understanding of the full confession that would be required.

He listened without a word, his chin resting on his steepled fingers. The smoke from his pipe, which he had lit with a slow and measured ritual, rose in a placid column, a single grey pillar in the still air of the room. When I had finished, when the whole sorry tale of my expedition and its moral collapse lay exposed between us, he was silent for a long time.

‘I see very well,’ he said at last, leaning forward, the lamp throwing his face into a landscape of stark shadows and bright, worn mesas of skin. ‘He is a purist.’

The diagnosis was so simple, so exact, it was as if he had lanced a wound I had not even known was festering. Our meeting had taken on the aspect of a doctor’s visit--Alistair, with his air of ancient knowledge, in his great chair behind the desk; I, the patient, twisted with a malady of the spirit--so that it seemed only natural to ask--

‘And what is the cure for it?’

He raised one long, ink-stained finger. ‘There is only one! Only one thing can from our own maps save us!’ The finger tapped the vellum with a sharp report. The problem, which had seemed so complex, became in that instant hideously simple--and utterly without solution. A pause descended. ‘Yes,’ said I, ‘but the question is not one of a cure. The question is how to carry on.’

He nodded, a deep and sorrowful agreement. ‘Ja! ja! In the end, to borrow from your own great poet: That is the question….’ He continued to nod, his eyes distant. ‘How to chart the course. Ach! How to chart.’

He rose from his chair and stood over the map, his hands hovering above its surface as if to warm them on its intricate lies.

‘We draw the lines so straight, so confident,’ he began again. ‘This magnificent chart tells you where the mountain is; it does not tell you that you will weep with exhaustion on its slope, that you will curse God in its shadow. Man…man wants to live on the map, on the clean paper where all is known. He wants the port to be so, and the jungle to be so….’ He swept a hand over the drawing. ‘He wants to be a hero, and he wants to be a saint--and every time he sleeps he sees himself as this fine fellow, a man so true he could set his compass by his own heart…. In a dream….’

He ran his hand along the edge of the vellum, the paper whispering under his touch. He seemed to have drifted away from me, into the geography of his own past, his voice taking on a distant, resonant quality as if spoken across a wide and desolate estuary.

‘And because you cannot live always on the map, there comes the true reckoning--the soul’s fever--the world’s pain. I tell you, my friend, it is a terrible thing to find your own chart is a lie, for the reason that you are not the cartographer you had dreamed you were, or not brave enough for the journey…. Ja!… And all the time you are such a fine fellow! Wie? Was? Gott im Himmel! How is this? Ha! ha! ha!’

The shadow hunched over the ghost of a coastline let out a short, bark-like laugh.

‘Yes! A very funny and terrible thing. A man who is born is given a map, a dream of the world, and he falls into the real country like a man falling from a ship. If he tries to climb back onto the map, onto the clean, dry paper, he will perish--nicht wahr?… No! I tell you! The way is to the wilderness submit yourself, and with the struggles of your heart and your hands in the mud make the deep, deep jungle sustain you. So if you ask me--how to chart the course?’

His voice rose with a sudden, startling force, as if he had found a new heading in the twilight of his thoughts. ‘I will tell you! For that too there is only one way.’

With a dry shuffling of his slippers, he moved back into the circle of the lamp, his body eclipsing the light for a moment before he reappeared. His extended hand pointed not at the map, but at my chest, a rigid accusation; his eyes were dark pools of certainty. But then his face faltered, the conviction that had illuminated him in the shadows seemed to douse itself in the lamplight. The hand dropped, and he took a step closer, laying it with a surprising gentleness on my arm. There were truths, he said, his voice again low and mournful, that had no symbols on any chart, only he had been alone with his own maps for so long that sometimes he forgot--he forgot. The light had shown him the folly of his own clear lines. He sat down heavily, burying his face in his hands. ‘And yet it is true--it is true. In the uncharted heart immerse.’… He spoke into his palms, not looking at me. ‘That was the way. To follow the dream, and then, to follow the dream into the mud--and so--ewig--usque ad finem….’ The whisper of his belief seemed to chart for me a vast and terrifying landscape, a wilderness at twilight--or was it, perhaps, at the first hint of dawn? One lacked the courage to be certain; but it was a beautiful and treacherous light, casting the impalpable poetry of its gloom over ravines--over boneyards. His own life had begun with a dream of clean lines; he had travelled far, by many routes, on strange coasts, and whatever he had sought he had done so without apology, and therefore without surrender and without regret. In so far, he was correct. That was the way, without doubt. Yet for all that, the great wilderness in which men lose their way remained a desolate place under the impalpable poetry of its twilight, shrouded in the centre, circled by a ring of fire as if surrounded by a sea of burning ships. When at last I found my voice it was to say that no one’s map could be more of a dream than his own.

He lifted his head slowly, and then looked at me with a sad and patient inquiry. It was the look of a man who possessed a perfect, beautiful chart of hell, and had chosen, long ago, to live there.

He stood up again, but this time his movements were different; they were not the slow, deliberate actions of a philosopher, but the restless, searching motions of a man trying to locate a specific tool. He went to a large teak cabinet that stood against the far wall, a dark monolith in the gloom. From it he produced not another butterfly, but a roll of yellowed parchment, tied with a faded ribbon that might once have been red. He laid it on the desk between us, and the dry rustle of the old paper was like the whisper of a ghost.

‘There are maps, and there are maps,’ he murmured, his fingers working at the brittle knot. ‘There are the charts of the Admiralty, full of facts and figures, depths and currents. They are made for ships. Then there are the maps of men, made for the soul. They are full of lies.’ The ribbon gave way, and he unrolled the parchment with the reverence of a priest handling a sacred text. It was a map, of a kind. A hand-drawn coastline, rendered in faded sepia ink, with islands like smudges of dirt and mountain ranges like the scratches of a nervous pen. It was a beautiful, terrible, and obviously useless thing. The compass rose in the corner was a work of art, a magnificent sunburst of lines and flourishes, but the degrees it marked were plainly whimsical. The lettering was exquisite, but the names were names from a poem or a fever-dream: the ‘Bay of Lost Intentions,’ the ‘Straits of Unknowing,’ ‘Port Regret.’

‘I drew this myself,’ he said, a strange, distant pride in his voice. ‘When I was very young. Before… before the professor, before the butterflies, before all this.’ His long finger traced a wavering line across the parchment. ‘This is a map of a place that never was. But I believed in it. I believed in it so much that I sailed a leaky schooner for six months, with a crew of scoundrels, looking for this very coast. I had nothing but this lie to guide me.’ He looked up from the map, his eyes fixing me with a new intensity. ‘And do you know what? We found nothing. Sickness. Storms. Mutiny. A great nothing. And yet… it was the making of me. Because at the end, when the food was gone, and the water was foul, and the crew had taken the only longboat, I was left alone with my map. This beautiful, perfect lie.’

He paused, letting the weight of his words settle in the silent room. ‘I had to burn it,’ he said softly. ‘Piece by piece. For warmth. On the last night, before a Dutch patrol vessel found me by chance, I burned the compass rose. I watched all the perfect lines turn to black ash. And in the light of my burning dream, I saw the real world for the first time. Cold. Empty. A wilderness. And I knew, in that moment, what I had to do. Not to find a new map. No. But to learn how to live in the wilderness without one.’

He leaned back, his story told, and gestured from the burnt, imaginary map to me. ‘So, you come to me to describe your specimen. This man. Tell me of the map he made for himself, the one he now finds is a lie. What is the name of his Port Regret?’

The directness of the question, after so much philosophy, was like a sudden light in a dark room, making me blink. I saw that he was no longer merely a thinker, a collector. He was a physician of the soul, and he had just finished explaining the nature of the disease; now he was demanding to see the patient.

‘His map,’ I began slowly, the words feeling heavy and inadequate, ‘was a map of honour. It was a very simple chart. Drawn with a straight rule. There was only one route, and it was the correct one. The line of duty, of fidelity, of… of a certain idea of conduct.’ I faltered, seeing in my mind’s eye the boyish, trusting face of my friend, a face that had believed so implicitly in the simple geography of right and wrong.

‘Ah,’ Stein nodded, a deep and knowing sound. ‘A map for a saint. The most dangerous kind. Because a saint can only go to one place, nicht wahr? To heaven. And if he takes one wrong turning, he is not in a different country. He is in hell. There is no in-between on such a map.’

‘That is it, precisely,’ I said, grateful for his understanding. ‘He took a wrong turning. In a moment of… of unthinking panic. He stepped off his clean, straight line. He jumped.’ The word hung in the air between us, small and ugly. ‘He found himself in the wilderness, as you say. And now… now he is trying to pretend he is still on the path. He walks through the mud, but he tells himself, and everyone else, that he is on a paved road. He wants to be that fine fellow, the one who never left the chart.’

Stein listened without moving, his face a mask of placid concentration. The smoke from his forgotten pipe, which he had begun to pack once more, rose in a thin, lazy spiral. When I had finished, a profound silence descended, broken only by the frantic drumming of a beetle against the lamp glass. It seemed to beat in time with the frantic pulse in my own throat.

He reached out his forefinger, the same long finger that had lectured me on the remedy for being ourselves, and he placed it deliberately in the centre of the hand-drawn map. He pressed down. The old parchment was thin, and where his finger rested, there was a dark, greasy smudge, a stain from some long-forgotten meal or drop of engine oil.

‘You see this mark?’ he asked, his voice returning to its gentle, didactic tone. ‘It has been there for forty years. When I first made it, I was horrified. It ruined the perfection of my line. My beautiful, lying line. I tried to erase it. I used sand. I used a knife. I only made it worse. A hole. A wound in the paper. It was a disaster. It was the first truth the map had ever told me.’

He lifted his finger, but the dark smudge remained, an indelible fact on a surface of fiction. ‘Your friend,’ he said, turning his gaze back to me, ‘is trying to erase the smudge. He is scraping at his own soul with a knife. He will make a hole, and he will fall through it into a nothingness from which no one returns. You must tell him this.’

‘Tell him what?’ I asked, my voice strained. ‘That he is damned? That there is no hope?’

‘Hope!’ he exclaimed, and for the first time, there was a spark of something like anger in his eye. ‘Hope is a word for a map of a place that does not exist! It is a name on a liar’s chart! No! You will not tell him of hope. You will tell him of the smudge!’

He stood up so quickly that his chair grated against the floor. He began to pace the small circle of lamplight, his slippers whispering on the boards, a tall, prowling shadow. ‘He wants to be that fine fellow? The man on the straight path? Good! Let him be. He must make it the centre of his new world. It is not a stain to be removed. It is a landmark! It is a mountain! It is the capital city of the country of himself! All roads on his new map must lead to it, or from it. He must not hide it. He must navigate by it!’

His voice had grown loud, ringing with the force of his conviction. He was no longer a gentle collector; he was a prophet, his face alight with a fierce, austere fire. ‘He wants to be a man of honour? Ja! Then he must be honourable about his dishonour. He must own it. He must live with it, not as a secret shame, but as a known truth. Like a man who has lost a leg. He does not pretend he can still run a race. He gets a wooden peg, and he learns to walk with a limp. And everyone can see the limp! It is the limp that shows he has survived. It is the limp that is his truth.’

He stopped his pacing and stood before me, his hands clasped behind his back, his head bowed as if in thought. The outburst had exhausted him. When he spoke again, his voice was quieter, tinged with a deep and abiding sorrow.

‘The destructive element… the uncharted heart… you immerse yourself. But you do not drown. You learn to breathe the water. This is what it means. You do not deny the abyss. You build your house on the edge of it. You tell your friend… you tell him that the only way to deserve the dream of himself is to accept the fact of himself. The whole fact. The jump. The mud. The fear. All of it. He must carry his own wilderness with him. Not as a burden, but as his kingdom.’

He went back to his chair and sank into it, the energy draining out of him, leaving him looking old and frail in the yellow light. He picked up the long-stemmed pipe again and this time succeeded in lighting it. A great cloud of fragrant smoke erupted, momentarily obscuring his face. When it cleared, his expression was once more placid, thoughtful, the face of the collector of beautiful, dead things.

For many, the disease is easier to bear.’ He looked at me, a long, searching look. ‘You will have to be a good friend. To give him such a medicine. He may hate you for it. For it is a bitter taste. The taste of truth.’

The frail wings of the butterfly in its case seemed to quiver in the heat from the lamp. I thought of my friend, my ‘specimen,’ lost in his own particular wilderness, trying so desperately to read a map that had already been consumed by the fires of his own actions. Stein’s words had not offered a solution, not a path out of the jungle. He had offered something far more terrible, and perhaps, far more true: a way to live within it. A way to be.

‘And you, Stein?’ I finally asked, my own voice sounding strange to me. ‘This… this remedy. Have you taken it yourself?’

He drew on his pipe, his eyes half-closed. The smoke curled around his head like a halo of doubt. He took the pipe from his mouth and examined the bowl as if the answer might be found in the glowing embers.

‘Me?’ he said, and a slow, sad smile touched his lips. ‘I am the collector. I take the beautiful things that have already come to the end of their story. The butterfly who has had its day on the heap of dirt. The map that has led its last man to ruin. I describe them. I put them in glass cases. I keep them safe from the wilderness.’ He gestured around the room, at the serried ranks of his silent treasures. ‘This is my place. Not the jungle. But the museum of the jungle. It is a… compromise.’
